justice: Spatial resources are strongly allocated to motor traffic: multiple wide vehicle lanes dominate the right-of-way compared with the narrow visible sidewalk on the right.
Physical separation elements (median guardrail and a raised/curbed planted strip) organize space clearly, but they also limit flexible crossing opportunities for people on foot.

Accessibility is uncertain because curb ramps, tactile paving, and marked pedestrian crossings are not visible in the scene; the sidewalk is present but its barrier-free continuity cannot be verified from this view.
safety: A continuous median guardrail reduces risky mid-block crossings and helps prevent head-on conflicts between opposing traffic streams.
Clear lane markings and a straight, open sightline improve predictability for drivers and reduce sudden maneuvers.
A separated sidewalk with a curb and a planted buffer strip provides pedestrians some protection from moving vehicles, though the road width may still encourage higher vehicle speeds.
livability: The streetscape reads as a through-corridor: long blocks, wide carriageway, and limited visible destinations at ground level reduce street life and lingering activities.
No benches, kiosks, plazas, or active frontage are visible along the right-side building edge, limiting opportunities for social interaction and rest.
Pedestrian presence and amenities are minimal in the frame (no visible bus stop, crosswalk, or storefront activity), which weakens perceived everyday convenience for non-drivers.
sustainability: Substantial street trees and planted strips along the right side and in the median contribute to urban greenery and potential air-quality/heat mitigation benefits.
The roadway design appears car-oriented (wide lanes, multi-lane cross-section), which can induce driving and raise transport emissions relative to more multimodal designs.
Lack of visible cycling infrastructure (no bike lane markings or protection) reduces support for low-carbon travel by bicycle.
aesthetics: Consistent street lighting, orderly lane markings, and clean pavement create a tidy, well-maintained visual impression.
Mature trees and continuous green planting (right-side canopy and median greenery) add visual softness and improve streetscape quality.
The corridor has strong linear perspective and coherence (uniform roadway geometry and repeated lamp posts), though the wide asphalt surface makes the scene feel somewhat monotonous.
comfort: Tree canopy on the right side can provide intermittent shade and improved thermal comfort for sidewalk users, but much of the corridor remains exposed due to the wide roadway.
The planting strip and curb create a psychological buffer from traffic, improving comfort for people walking compared with a sidewalk directly adjacent to moving cars.

Noise and stress may remain moderate because traffic lanes are wide and the street functions as an arterial; no visible noise barriers or calming features (e.g., narrow lanes, raised crossings) are present.
walkability: A sidewalk is present on the right with a planted buffer, supporting basic pedestrian movement along the corridor.
Crossing support appears weak: no zebra crossing, pedestrian signals, or refuge islands are visible, and the median guardrail discourages convenient crossing.
The large road width and arterial character increase walking deterrence (long exposure at intersections and fewer mid-block access options).
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane markings, colored pavement, or protected cycling space is visible, reducing perceived and actual cycling safety.
The multi-lane, high-speed-feeling road environment increases speed differential risk for cyclists mixing with traffic.
Physical separation in the corridor is designed for vehicles vs. pedestrians (curbs/guardrails), but there is no analogous protected facility or clear route for cyclists.
